## The idea

Add seven semitones to C and you reach G. Repeat the operation modulo twelve and
the sequence visits every pitch class before returning to C. Music books draw
this cycle as the *circle of fifths*. The diagram is a visualisation of a tiny
generator.

The order earns its place because neighbouring major keys share six of their
seven pitch classes. C major and G major differ only at F versus F-sharp. G and D
differ only at C versus C-sharp. The circle therefore stores proximity as
adjacency. It also predicts key-signature counts and gives each major key's
relative minor three semitones below it.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :piano

define :major_pitch_classes do |root|
  [0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11].map { |offset| (root + offset) % 12 }
end

circle = 12.times.map { |index| (index * 7) % 12 }
names = [:c, :g, :d, :a, :e, :b, :fs, :cs, :gs, :ds, :as, :f]

circle.each_with_index do |pitch_class, index|
  next_class = circle[(index + 1) % circle.length]
  shared = major_pitch_classes(pitch_class) & major_pitch_classes(next_class)
  relative_minor = (pitch_class - 3) % 12
  puts "#{names[index]} pc=#{pitch_class} relative_minor=#{relative_minor} shared=#{shared.length}"

  play_chord major_pitch_classes(pitch_class).first(3).map { |pc| pc + 60 },
    release: 0.65, amp: 0.7
  sleep 1
end
```

The roots move by a perfect fifth while the chords trace a long cycle back to
C. The log reports six shared pitch classes for every adjacent pair. Near the
end, enharmonic spelling becomes awkward because pitch-class integers cannot
choose between F-sharp and G-flat. The `names` array carries that separate
spelling decision.

## Change one thing

1. Change `7` to `5` in the circle generator. You travel by descending fifths,
   or ascending fourths, and visit the same pitch classes in reverse order.
2. Print the set difference between adjacent scales as well as the intersection.
   Moving clockwise replaces degree 4 of the old key with the new leading tone.
   Hear that changed pitch before each chord.
3. Start the rendered chord tones one octave lower. The pitch-class structure
   stays fixed while register changes the weight of the cycle.

## Why it works

Seven and twelve are coprime. Repeated addition of seven modulo twelve therefore
visits all twelve residues before repeating. If the step shared a factor with
twelve, the cycle would close early. Adding six, for example, alternates between
two pitch classes.

Major scales are also generated structures. Transposing the interval set
`[0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11]` by seven changes only one member after reduction modulo
twelve. That high overlap explains why adjacent keys offer smooth routes for
modulation. It also explains the sharp sequence: each clockwise step preserves
six notes and raises the remaining one.

The relative minor calculation uses `root - 3`, reduced modulo twelve. Relative
major and minor keys share a key signature and pitch collection, though they
centre different tonics. The integer tells you the pitch class; a spelling table
still has to decide whether `6` appears as F-sharp or G-flat. Lesson 10's second
field remains necessary.

The rendered chords in this program use the first three sorted pitch classes,
which is a crude voicing rather than a faithful root-position triad. Modular sets
lose octave order. For harmonic playback, recover each scale degree above the
current root before selecting degrees 1, 3, and 5. The pitch-class version is
kept here because intersection and adjacency are the objects under inspection.

## Take it further

Write `key_record(index)` for positions from `-7` through `7`. Return the tonic
spelling, accidental count, accidental type, relative minor spelling, and the
two neighbouring keys. Generate the values from circle position rather than a
fifteen-row lookup table. Print the records from seven flats through seven
sharps, then play each key's tonic triad in that order.
